text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.3. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.3.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.3 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 18 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
This looks like a public goods game with an interesting payoff structure—each member keeps some tokens privately or contributes to the group account, and I'm working through how my private tokens and the group total each affect my own points, including that negative externality others' private holdings impose on me.

Group contributions create no cross-externalities since the 0.3 return goes only to the contributor, while private tokens have a stronger negative spillover (-0.3 to each of three others). So socially, group contribution yields more total welfare (0.3 vs 0.1 per token), but individually keeping tokens private still dominates since 1 > 0.3 per token for me. This makes full defection the Nash equilibrium even though full cooperation is socially optimal—with 10 repeated rounds, sustained cooperation would require conditional strategies, though I only observe the group total, not individual contributions.

For round 1, I'll contribute all 20 tokens as a cooperative signal to maximize group welfare and encourage reciprocal cooperation, even though a pure self-interest calculation would favor defection or partial contribution.
